extracted.intended_audience: instructor trainers, instructional consultants, and university/college instructors (especially mathematics), who conduct classroom observations and collect student feedback
extracted.subtask_description: Procedures and evaluative guidelines for arranging, conducting, documenting, and following up on classroom observations and student-feedback sessions (including peer visits and instructor-led midterm feedback) aimed at improving teaching practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Arranging the visit
rubrics_metrics.description: Well in advance of the intended visit, contact the instructor to be visited, and set up a day and time for the visit. Confirm that the instructor doesn’t have something like a test planned for that day. Explain the process and assure the instructor that the feedback will be kept confidential.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While explaining the process, cover five items: (1) Emphasize that the student feedback session will take between twenty and twenty-five minutes, and that the instructor should leave the room with at least twenty minutes remaining in class; (2) Ask the instructor if there is anything about the class, or the way it is run, on which the instructor would specifically like feedback; (3) Ask the instructor to acknowledge your presence in the class, or introduce you and the purpose of the visit to the class; (4) Set up a date, time and place to give the students’ feedback to the instructor and set aside an hour for the follow-up meeting; (5) Ask if an overhead projector is available and, if so, bring two blank transparencies and a marker.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conducting the observation
rubrics_metrics.description: Arrive early for the class, and find a seat that will allow you to observe the instructor and the majority of students with ease. Introduce yourself if necessary and confirm timing for the feedback session. During the first part of the class, observe the class just as in an observational visit, taking notes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Observe both what the instructor does and what students do. Take notes you feel are relevant and treat this as an observational visit until the feedback portion begins. Confirm that the feedback session will begin between twenty and twenty-five minutes before the end of class.

rubrics_metrics.name: Facilitating the student feedback session
rubrics_metrics.description: Form the class into groups of three or four students, ask each group to appoint a recorder, and distribute response sheets asking students to 'List the major strengths of this course (What is helping you learn in the course?)' and 'List changes that could be made in the course to assist you in learning.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Encourage specificity and examples; give groups five to seven minutes to discuss; circulate and keep groups on-task; note at least one group listing a positive strength to start the report-out. If available, set up an overhead labeled 'Strengths' and 'Changes' (or two columns on the board). Go around each group asking for contributions; record strengths verbatim; on each suggested item, check for majority opinion by a quick show of hands and only record items agreed to by a majority. Clarify vague suggestions by asking for examples. If instructor-requested issues were not mentioned, ask about them. End on time, collect all sheets, check accuracy, and erase boards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Writing the report and preparing for the meeting
rubrics_metrics.description: Type student comments from the two final forms or overheads onto two separate pages, one for Strengths and one for Changes. Order items from most significant to least significant and omit comments judged unnecessary or inappropriate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consult observational notes and group sheets to find specific examples to substantiate student-raised issues. Pick two or three key issues to emphasize in the meeting (rather than many small issues). If the instructor requested focus on particular issues, be prepared to address them. Sample reports are provided in the text for reference.

rubrics_metrics.name: Meeting with the instructor
rubrics_metrics.description: Meet with the instructor soon after the visit (while the session is still fresh) to discuss observations and the student feedback report.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Thank the instructor; invite them to describe how the class went and course goals. When sharing the report, give the 'Strengths' sheet first (to avoid the instructor focusing only on changes). Allow time for reading and clarification; draw on specific student examples and your observations. Ask the instructor for reactions, how comments fit course goals, and what changes they can or will make. Focus discussion on two or three most important issues. If some student suggestions are unreasonable, encourage the instructor to explain publicly why changes won't be made. Help the instructor plan a brief (5–10 minute) response to the class that acknowledges feedback, explains implementations or reasons for not implementing certain suggestions, and communicates next steps.

rubrics_metrics.name: Following up after the visit
rubrics_metrics.description: Check back with the instructor after a couple of weeks to see how the class is going and how changes have affected the learning environment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Some instructors resist follow-up; balance persistence with respect. Follow-up can identify whether implemented changes were effective and provide continued support or advice as needed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Midterm student feedback form content
rubrics_metrics.description: A short form used by small groups asking: I. 'List the major strengths of the course. (What is helping you learn in the course?)' with space for Explanation/Example; II. 'List changes that could be made in the course to assist you in learning. Please explain how suggested changes could be made.' with space for 'Ways your instructor can make changes.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Forms instruct groups to reach consensus, be explicit, use examples, and have a recorder write down agreed comments. Typical form has numbered slots (1–5) under Strengths and Changes for group responses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Advantages of student feedback visits
rubrics_metrics.description: Student feedback visits give students an opportunity to voice opinions during the semester, often pick up things outside observers miss, and because items are open-ended they reveal what is most important to students.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Other advantages: consensus-building removes isolated extreme opinions; if done correctly, the activity can improve student morale and satisfaction with the course; feedback comes straight from students and can be used to improve the course while it still benefits them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disadvantages of student feedback visits
rubrics_metrics.description: Some instructors may not take responses seriously unless precise clarification is available; a lone observer may be overwhelmed by many classes or rude students; instructors may feel threatened or resent being evaluated by students; students can make unrealistic or non-constructive suggestions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Other cautions: including unrealistic suggestions undermines credibility; some students may use it to continue complaining; instructors may consider collection of feedback a waste of time; students may have high expectations that changes will be implemented and may resent lack of response.

rubrics_metrics.name: Procedure for collecting student feedback without a visit (instructor-led)
rubrics_metrics.description: When an observer visit is impractical, the instructor can collect feedback by dividing the class into groups of three to four, handing each group a recording sheet, leaving the classroom, and having groups discuss strengths and suggested changes for five to seven minutes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Each group appoints a recorder who records points the group agrees on; a student collects the papers at the end and returns them to the instructor. Sample sheets mirror the ones used in facilitated visits. This method is more convenient but potentially less effective than an outside-facilitated visit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Instructor's tasks when collecting own student feedback
rubrics_metrics.description: When collecting feedback without an outside facilitator, the instructor should: set aside 15 minutes, explain the spirit and intention of the exercise, describe the process, appoint a student to collect papers, tell students the instructor will respond in a few days, leave the room, and later formulate a response plan.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Items to emphasize when explaining: the exercise gives students a voice now; it is anonymous and confidential; both positives and suggestions are requested; responses should reflect group consensus; the instructor values and will take opinions seriously; students should focus on aspects the instructor can control. The response plan could include: an acknowledgment of feedback; ideas for implementing changes; how to deal with impossible requests; how to make students aware of efforts; and how to establish whether changes were effective. Also: meet with another instructor to discuss the process, and when addressing students avoid defensiveness and explain reasoning when not implementing suggestions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Advantages of collecting your own student feedback
rubrics_metrics.description: Easier to arrange than an outside visit; useful for instructors who resist outside observation; usually takes less class time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These advantages can increase convenience and uptake among instructors who refuse visits, though they may come at the cost of richness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disadvantages of collecting your own student feedback
rubrics_metrics.description: Feedback may be less rich and useful without an observer to clarify meaning; there is no filtration of inappropriate or rude suggestions; it can be hard to find priorities without an outside facilitator; instructors may take comments personally and be discouraged.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Without an external facilitator, consensus-building and prioritization are harder and the instructor risks being overwhelmed by negative or unfiltered comments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Procedure for implementing a program of peer visits
rubrics_metrics.description: Pair instructors and have them conduct observational visits for each other, schedule visits close together, and meet to share feedback soon after the second visitation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prepare instructors by explaining goals and giving handouts that can be adapted from the chapter's goals. Give guidelines on conducting the process and basic observational/feedback skills. Break guidelines into: (1) setting up, (2) the visit, (3) writing the report and planning for the meeting, and (4) the meeting. Decide on a mechanism for feedback (written reports or round-table exchanges).

rubrics_metrics.name: Advantages of peer visits
rubrics_metrics.description: Peer visits can lend a collaborative spirit, provide peer support, require less coordinator time, reduce fear (observer not in authority), and expose instructors to alternative teaching strategies while developing observation and feedback skills.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because observers become observed and vice versa, hierarchical feelings are reduced; coordinators can still learn from reports and exchanges.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disadvantages of peer visits
rubrics_metrics.description: Peer visits may lead some instructors to shirk responsibility since a coordinator is not directly involved; inexperienced observers may not provide constructive feedback; some pairs may become competitive and focus on shortcomings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Programs should consider training or guidelines to reduce these risks and ensure accountability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Encouraging instructor cooperation
rubrics_metrics.description: To encourage instructor participation in visits, keep the process entirely confidential and clearly communicate this, and use visits for assessment not evaluation (especially for beginning instructors).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Give constructive, compassionate, credible, and concrete feedback; concentrate on things that are going right and on deficiencies within reach of improvement; use your experience to speak to instructors' mathematical and pedagogical sensibilities; be efficient and persistent in contacting instructors who avoid visits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Encouraging student cooperation during feedback sessions
rubrics_metrics.description: Alleviate student resistance by having the instructor tell students beforehand that their feedback is welcomed and valued, and that it can favorably affect changes in the class.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explain that collected patterns may be used to improve departmental teaching; be polite, in control, and extremely efficient; explain the procedure clearly and conduct it confidently to reduce contempt or cynicism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anticipating and preparing for problematic situations
rubrics_metrics.description: Facilitators should reflect on what they will do if common unpleasant situations arise (e.g., instructor ignores contact, cancels due to a test, gives a surprise test, continues past allotted time, students attempt to leave, students refuse to form groups, disruptive students take over discussion, personal attacks, inconsistent summary sheets, instructor fails to attend follow-up, defensive instructor, peer pairs fail to execute visits, competitive hostility).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prepare responses and contingency plans for each example situation (e.g., re-assert timing needs, confirm logistics in advance, collect and verify sheets, re-schedule meetings promptly, have protocols for disruptive students, and persistently attempt contact when instructors avoid visits).

rubrics_metrics.name: General principles for successful visits
rubrics_metrics.description: Use visits for instructors' professional growth rather than evaluation; plan to do visits early in the semester; be well prepared, supportive, credible, and thorough in feedback.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emphasize confidentiality and the developmental purpose of visits to minimize instructors' apprehension. Recognize time and energy costs for trainers but prioritize visits as a vital part of integrated professional development programs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Suggested checklist categories and rubrics for classroom observation
rubrics_metrics.description: Existing checklists arrange observer questions into categories such as importance and suitability of content, organization of content, presentation style, establishing and maintaining contact with students, and questioning ability. Other rubrics list: planning and organization, classroom management, methods and techniques, and personal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These categories can be adapted into observation instruments. Note caveat: some professional standards are decontextualized (e.g., 'Use of the board, overhead, and corresponding seat work was very effective') and observers should define what 'effective' means in context and identify observable evidence.
